text: About 375 million years ago, Earth had no animals with legs walking on land. Plants were spreading, and insects' relatives scuttled about, but backboned animals still lived in water.

Some fish in shallow, warm streams had thick, fleshy fins with bones inside, unlike the thin fins of a goldfish. These lobe-finned fish also had lungs as well as gills. Over millions of years, their fins became stronger, able to prop up the body. Their heads gained necks. Eventually their descendants walked out of the water. Every animal with four limbs today, from frogs to elephants to you, comes from them.

sec.t:
Scientists have several ideas, and they may all be partly right. Shallow streams could be warm and low in oxygen, so simple [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] that gulped air helped. Big fish hunted in deeper water, so the shallows were safer. And land offered food: plants and creeping bugs that nothing else was eating yet.

Early four-legged animals like Acanthostega, about 365 million years ago, still lived mostly in water. Acanthostega had eight fingers on each front limb, and Ichthyostega had seven toes on its back feet. Five fingers became the standard later.

In 2010, scientists described fossil footprints from a quarry at Zachełmie in Poland. They were made by an animal with four limbs, about 390 million years ago. That's older than Tiktaalik.

So Tiktaalik wasn't the very first. It was a late survivor of a group that had already started on the path. The footprints show that four-legged animals appeared earlier than the bones suggested, and some scientists think they may have walked on tidal flats by the sea as well as in streams. The hunt for older fossils goes on.

Some fish still try out life on land. Mudskippers in Indian [[@mangroves|mangroves]], like those of the Sundarbans, skip across the mud on their fins and breathe through their skin and mouth. Lungfish in Africa, South America and Australia can gulp air, and African lungfish survive dry seasons buried in mud.

The climbing perch of Indian ponds can wriggle across land from one pond to another. In some places it's said to climb trees, but that's mostly a story. These fish aren't our ancestors, but they show how the first steps could have worked.

Your body keeps the record too. Your arm [[@bones|bones]] follow the one-bone, two-bones, many-bones plan of Tiktaalik's fin. Some scientists even think your hiccups are a leftover reflex shared with tadpoles and air-breathing fish. It's one more clue in the long story of [[evolution|evolution]] that leads from Arctic streams to [[@human-evolution|humans]].

text: Mary Anning was one of the most important fossil hunters who ever lived. She grew up poor in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England, and spent her life searching the crumbling cliffs for fossils to sell.

She found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised by scientists, the first complete [[@marine-reptiles-plesiosaur|plesiosaur]], and Britain's first [[@pterosaurs|pterosaur]]. Her finds helped convince scientists that whole kinds of animals had lived long ago and died out. Because she was a woman and had little money, she was rarely given credit in her lifetime.

Fossils are easier to see when they are cold

st.reveal: Storms and heavy rain made the soft cliffs crumble and slide, exposing fresh fossils. Mary had to collect them quickly before the sea washed them away. It was also dangerous work, and a landslide once nearly killed her.

sec.t:
Mary was born in 1799. Her father, Richard, was a carpenter who also collected fossils from the beach and sold them to visitors. He took Mary and her brother Joseph along with him. A famous story comes from even earlier. In 1800, when Mary was a baby, [[@lightning|lightning]] struck a tree in Lyme Regis where people were sheltering. The woman holding her was killed, but Mary survived. Local people called the fossils "curiosities", and spiral [[@ammonites|ammonites]] were known as "snakestones".

Her father died in 1810, leaving the family in debt. Selling fossils became a way to put food on the table. Mary learned to read, and taught herself geology and anatomy from books and papers, sometimes copying them out by hand.

Mary did more than dig. She cleaned and studied her fossils carefully, and visiting scientists often asked her opinion. She noticed that strange stones often found inside ichthyosaur skeletons were full of fish scales and small bones. They were [[@dino-poop|fossil poo]]. The geologist William Buckland published the idea, and the stones were named coprolites.

Her work was dangerous. The cliffs at Lyme Regis are soft and slip after storms, which is exactly when new fossils appear. In 1833, a landslide killed her dog, Tray, at her side.

Scientists in London bought her fossils, wrote papers about them and named the animals. Mary was usually not mentioned. The Geological Society of London did not [[@equality|admit women]], so she could not attend its meetings. She did receive some support near the end of her life, and after her death in 1847, the Society honoured her. In 2010, the Royal Society, Britain's oldest science academy, named her among the ten British women who most influenced the history of science.

Today, her ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are displayed at the [[@dino-museums|Natural History Museum]] in London. The coast she searched is part of the Jurassic Coast, a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]]. In 2022, a statue of Mary was unveiled in Lyme Regis, after a campaign started by a girl named Evie Swire when she was 11. It shows Mary with her hammer and her dog, looking down at the beach.

text: If Earth stopped spinning in an instant, it would be a disaster. The ground would stop, but the air, the oceans and everything not tied down would keep moving east at the old speed. At the equator, that's about 1,670 km/h, faster than a passenger jet. Winds that strong would scrape the land bare.

If Earth slowed down gently over thousands of years, things would be stranger but survivable in places. A single "day" would last a whole year, the oceans would slide towards the poles, and a giant continent would appear around the equator. Neither is going to happen. Earth is slowing, but only by about 2 thousandths of a second each century.

sec.h: You are moving faster than a jet
sec.t:
Earth turns once every 24 hours or so. The equator is about 40,000 km around, so the ground there moves at about 1,670 km/h.

The further from the equator you are, the shorter your circle, and the slower you move. Bengaluru rushes east at about 1,600 km/h, Delhi at about 1,470 km/h and New York at about 1,270 km/h. At the North Pole you simply turn on the spot.

We don't feel it because everything moves together: the ground, the air and you. It's like sitting on a smooth train where a cup of chai stays still on the table.

sec.h: A slow stop: the new map
sec.t:
Because Earth spins, it bulges at the middle. The equator is about 21 km further from Earth's centre than the poles are. The oceans bulge too, held in place by the spin.

In 2010, a scientist at the mapping company Esri, Witold Fraczek, modelled what would happen without the spin. Gravity would pull the water towards the poles, forming two great polar oceans. Around the middle, the sea floor would rise out of the water to form one giant continent stretching right around the planet.

India would sit on that new land, joined to Africa and Southeast Asia by dry ground. The Himalaya would look even taller from the new low plains.

If Earth stopped turning but kept circling the Sun, each place would face the Sun for about six months, then face away for six months. One day and one night would together last a whole year.

The day side would bake for months and the night side would freeze. The air between them would rush from hot to cold, creating new wind patterns. Plants and animals adapted to 24-hour days would struggle. [[@time-zones|Time zones]] would stop making sense, since noon would last for weeks.

Earth's spin makes moving air curve, an effect called the Coriolis effect. It is why [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]] and cyclones spin anticlockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it.

Without spin, storms wouldn't twist into those great spirals. Ocean currents, which carry warmth around the world, would change too. No one knows exactly what the new weather would be like.

Earth's [[@earth-magnet|magnetic field]] comes from molten iron swirling in the outer core. Most scientists think the planet's rotation helps organise that swirling. Venus spins extremely slowly and has no strong magnetic field of its own.

Without a magnetic shield, more particles from the Sun would reach the upper air, which could slowly strip some of it away. That part is still debated. Earth will keep spinning for billions of years, gradually slowed by the Moon, a story that begins with the question of [[@what-if-no-moon|what if there were no Moon]].

text: Aditya-L1 is India's first space observatory built to study the Sun. It was launched by ISRO in September 2023 and now watches [[@sun-what|the Sun]] from a special point in space called L1, about 1.5 million km from Earth. That is roughly four times as far as the Moon.

Its seven instruments study the Sun's surface, its outer layers and the stream of particles it blows into space. Scientists want to understand how the Sun works and how its storms affect Earth. Those storms can damage [[@satellites-help|satellites]], disturb radio and GPS signals, and in extreme cases harm power grids.

st.prompt: Why did ISRO send Aditya-L1 so far away, instead of keeping it close to Earth?

options.t: From there, Earth and the Moon never get in the way of the Sun
It is much closer to the Sun, so the photos are bigger
Earth's gravity does not reach that far

st.reveal: A satellite orbiting Earth spends part of every orbit in Earth's shadow. At L1, Aditya-L1 sits between Earth and the Sun and can watch the Sun all day, every day. It is only about 1 per cent closer to the Sun than Earth is.

d.try: Tape a heavy coin to one end of a ruler and a light coin to the other. Balance the ruler on one finger and find the balance point. It will be much nearer the heavy coin. L1 is a balance point too, much nearer Earth than the Sun. Remember never to look directly at the Sun.
myth: The Sun is a giant ball of fire, burning like a campfire.

Nothing on the Sun is burning in the everyday sense, because burning needs oxygen. In its core, hydrogen is squeezed so hard that it fuses into helium, releasing enormous energy. That process is called nuclear fusion.
facts: Aditya is a Sanskrit name for the Sun

sec.t:
Between Earth and the Sun there is a place where the pull of the two balances in a special way. A spacecraft there can stay lined up with Earth and the Sun, moving round the Sun with us, using very little fuel. This is the first Lagrange point, or L1, named after the 18th-century mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange, who worked out where such points must be.

Aditya-L1 doesn't sit perfectly still. It loops around L1 in a big, slow orbit called a halo orbit. It took about four months to get there after launch.

From L1, nothing ever blocks the Sun. A satellite near Earth passes through Earth's shadow, and even the biggest [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] on the ground lose the Sun every night. Aditya-L1 watches it nonstop.

The Sun's outer layer, the corona, is a puzzle. The Sun's visible surface is about 5,500°C. The corona, far above it, is well over a million degrees. It is a bit like walking away from a fire and feeling the air get hotter.

The corona is normally hidden by the glare of the Sun, and on Earth it can only be seen properly during a total [[@eclipses|eclipse]], for a few minutes at a time. Aditya-L1 carries an instrument called the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph, built by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru. It contains a small disc that blocks the bright face of the Sun, making an artificial eclipse that lasts as long as scientists like.

Another instrument, the Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope, built with the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics in Pune, photographs the Sun in ultraviolet light our eyes can't see.

Sometimes the Sun throws out a huge cloud of electrically charged gas, called a coronal mass ejection. If one heads our way, it can reach Earth in one to three days. Aditya-L1 sits upstream, so it can sample these particles before they reach us.

When they hit Earth's magnetic field, they can trigger brilliant [[@aurora|auroras]]. In May 2024, a powerful solar storm, which Aditya-L1 observed, produced auroras seen as far south as [[@ladakh|Ladakh]].

{{story:telegraph}}

The biggest storm on record struck in September 1859, now called the Carrington Event. Auroras appeared over the Caribbean, and [[@telegraph|telegraph]] wires sparked. Some operators found they could send messages with their batteries unplugged. A storm like that today could knock out satellites and power grids, so forecasting [[@space-weather|space weather]] matters.

Aditya-L1 joins other solar observatories at L1, including SOHO, run by the European Space Agency and NASA since 1996. Having several spacecraft watching with different instruments helps scientists cross-check what they see.

The mission also gives Indian students and scientists their own data. ISRO releases Aditya-L1's observations publicly, so researchers in universities across the country can study the Sun without waiting to borrow someone else's spacecraft.

text: Stars are born in giant clouds of gas and dust called [[nebula|nebulas]]. Gravity slowly pulls clumps of the cloud together. As a clump shrinks, its centre gets hotter and more squashed, until it reaches about 10 million °C. Then hydrogen [[atom|atoms]] begin to fuse into helium, releasing enormous energy. A star switches on.

A star dies when its fuel runs low. A star like the Sun swells up, puffs off its outer layers and shrinks into a small, hot leftover called a [[@star-life-cycle|white dwarf]]. Much heavier stars explode.

Sun-like stars puff off their outsides and shrink to a white dwarf. Giant stars explode as supernovas.

Compare the orange-red star at one shoulder, Betelgeuse, with the blue-white star at the opposite knee, Rigel. The colour tells you the temperature. Blue-white is hotter than orange-red.

Nothing is burning in a star the way wood burns. Stars shine because of nuclear fusion, where light atoms are squeezed together to make heavier ones, releasing huge amounts of energy.

sec.t:
You can see a star nursery with your own eyes. Below the three stars of Orion's belt hangs a fuzzy patch called the Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away. Through binoculars it looks like a faint glowing cloud. Inside it, thousands of young stars are forming right now.

In 1995, the [[@hubble|Hubble]] telescope photographed towering columns of gas in the Eagle Nebula, nicknamed the Pillars of Creation. In 2022, the [[@webb-telescope|Webb telescope]] looked again in infrared light, which passes through dust. It revealed newborn stars glowing inside the pillars like lamps in fog.

Once a star switches on, it spends most of its life steadily turning hydrogen into helium. Gravity squeezes inward, and the heat from fusion pushes outward. The two balance.

How long this lasts depends on the star's mass. The [[@sun-what|Sun]] is about halfway through a life of roughly 10 billion years. Bigger stars burn through their fuel much faster and live only a few million years. Small, cool red dwarfs can last far longer than the universe has existed so far.

Colour gives away a star's temperature. [[@stars-colours|Blue-white stars]] are the hottest. Orange and red stars are cooler.

{{story:body-cells}}

When a Sun-like star runs low on hydrogen in its core, it swells into a red giant, hundreds of times wider than before. In about 5 billion years, the Sun will do this, and may swallow [[@mercury-planet|Mercury]] and Venus. Then it will gently push off its outer layers into a glowing shell of gas. What's left is a white dwarf, about as big as Earth but as heavy as a star, slowly cooling for billions of years.

A star more than about eight times the Sun's mass ends far more violently. Its core collapses in less than a second, and the star blows apart in a [[@supernova|supernova]]. For a few weeks, one exploding star can outshine a whole galaxy.

In the year 1054, Chinese astronomers recorded a new star bright enough to see in daylight. Today, telescopes pointed at that spot see the Crab Nebula, the expanding wreck of that explosion. At its centre spins a tiny, superdense [[@space-weird-neutron-spoon|neutron star]]. If the leftover core is heavy enough, it becomes a [[@black-holes|black hole]].

The Indian scientist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar worked out the limit for how heavy a white dwarf can be before it must collapse. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983.

The first stars had almost nothing to work with but hydrogen and helium. Over billions of years, stars built heavier elements, like carbon, oxygen, calcium and iron, and scattered them into space when they died. New stars and planets formed from that enriched dust, including the Sun and Earth.

So almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star. The astronomer Carl Sagan put it simply: we are made of star-stuff.

text: Earth would still be a planet with air, oceans and seasons. But a lot would feel different. Nights would be much darker. Ocean [[@tides|tides]] would be about a third as high, because the Moon causes about two-thirds of them. There would be no solar eclipses, and no month as we know it.

Over billions of years, the bigger changes would stack up. Our day might be much shorter, and Earth's tilt might swing about more wildly, making seasons far more extreme. Scientists are still arguing about how wild that swing would be.

d.try: Hold a ball (the Earth) and a small orange (the Moon) at arm's length. Put the orange about 30 Earth-widths away from the ball. That is the real scale gap between them, and it is much wider than most pictures show.
myth: The Moon only affects the ocean, not the land.
The Moon pulls on solid rock too. The ground under your feet rises and falls by about 20 to 30 cm twice a day, but because everything around you moves with it, you never notice.

sec.t:
A full moon is the brightest thing in our night sky after the Sun. Without it, nights would be dark every single night, like the darkest new-moon night you've ever seen.

Many animals rely on moonlight. Some dung beetles find their way using light from the night sky. Studies of lions in Tanzania found they make more kills on the darkest nights, when prey can't see them coming.

On the Great Barrier Reef, many corals release their eggs together on a few nights after a full moon in spring. It is one of the largest spawning events on Earth. Without the Moon, they would need another signal.

The Moon acts like a gentle brake on Earth. The tides rub against the sea floor, and over time that friction slows our spin. Our day gets longer by about 2 thousandths of a second every century.

Long ago, days were shorter. Growth rings in fossil corals show that about 400 million years ago, a year had around 400 days, each about 22 hours long. Without the Moon braking it, Earth might still spin much faster today. Some estimates suggest a day of only 8 to 12 hours, though nobody can be sure.

Earth leans over at about 23.4 degrees. That tilt gives us [[@seasons-why|seasons]]. The Moon's pull helps keep the angle steady.

In 1993, a team led by French astronomer Jacques Laskar calculated that without the Moon, Earth's tilt could swing chaotically, from almost upright to lying nearly on its side. That would mean ice ages and scorching summers. Later studies suggested the swings would be slower and smaller than first feared. The debate is still going.

The word "month" comes from "moon". Many calendars still follow it. The Islamic calendar is fully lunar, which is why Eid moves about 11 days earlier each year. Hindu calendars count lunar days called tithis, so Diwali falls on a new-moon night and Holi near a full moon. Chinese New Year follows the Moon too.

Without a Moon, every one of these would have needed a different clock. The [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]] we use would look completely unfamiliar.

The Moon probably formed about 4.5 billion years ago, when a planet-sized object crashed into the young Earth and splashed rock into space. It wasn't guaranteed. Mercury and Venus have no moons at all.

And one day, very slowly, ours will appear smaller in the sky. As it drifts away, total solar eclipses will end, because the Moon will no longer cover the whole Sun. That will take hundreds of millions of years, and it is the same perfect fit that makes today's [[@eclipses|eclipses]] possible.

text: When a cat starts falling the wrong way up, its inner ear senses which way is down within a split second. The cat turns its head first, then twists its front half round while its back half stays almost still. A moment later it twists the back half to match. By the time it lands, its feet are underneath it, its back is arched and its legs are ready to soak up the bump.

The clever part is that it does all this in mid-air, with nothing to push against. Cats can manage it because their spines are very bendy and their collarbones float loose in muscle instead of locking the shoulders in place.

It swings its tail round like a propeller until it flips

st.reveal: The cat tucks its front legs and twists its front half one way, while its stretched-out back legs barely move. Then it swaps, tucking the back legs to turn the rear. Tailless cats can still do it, so the tail is only a small helper.

myth: Cats always land safely, so falls can't hurt them.

Cats are good at landing on their feet, but falls still injure many of them every year. Vets see so many cats hurt in falls from flats that they gave it a name, "high-rise syndrome". Windows and balconies need screens.

sec.t:
Here is how a cat cheats the rule. It bends in the middle, so it becomes two halves. It pulls its front legs in tight, which makes the front half easy to spin, like a skater pulling in their arms. At the same time it sticks its back legs out, which makes the back half hard to spin. The front swings round a long way, and the back turns only slightly the other way.

Then the cat swaps. Front legs out, back legs in. Now the rear half catches up. The total spin still adds up to zero, so physics is happy, but the cat ends up the right way round. Astronauts floating inside a space station have used a version of this to turn without grabbing anything.

In 1987, two New York vets studied 132 cats that had fallen from tall buildings, on average about five and a half storeys. Around 90 percent survived with treatment. Oddly, cats that fell from above seven storeys seemed to have fewer broken legs than those from lower down.

One idea is that a cat only reaches its top speed, about 95 km/h, after falling a few storeys. Once it stops speeding up, it relaxes and spreads its legs like a furry parachute, which slows it slightly and spreads out the landing. Other scientists point out a catch: cats that died in the fall were never taken to the vet, so they weren't counted. The truth is probably a mix of both.

The righting reflex makes sense for an animal that hunts in trees and on walls. Leopards, snow leopards and many [[@cats-big-small|wild cats]] do the same. Squirrels and some lizards can twist in the air as well.

A cat's light body helps a lot. The smaller you are, the slower you fall compared with your weight, which is why a mouse can survive a fall that would hurt a cat. This is part of the story of how [[@gravity-fall|gravity makes things fall]].

And the strangest part? A cat knows which way is down thanks to tiny fluid-filled chambers and loops in its [[@ears-hear|inner ear]]. You have almost exactly the same thing inside your own head.

text: A dog's nose is one of the best smell detectors on Earth. Many dogs have around 300 million smell receptors, special cells that catch scent molecules, compared with about 6 million in a human nose. The part of a dog's brain that handles smell is also much bigger, compared with its brain size, than ours.

Scientists usually say dogs smell 10,000 to 100,000 times better than people, though it is hard to measure exactly. One expert compared it to noticing a teaspoon of sugar stirred into two Olympic swimming pools. That is why dogs find bombs at airports, track missing people in forests and, in some studies, sniff out illnesses like diabetes or cancer.

Straight out the front of the nostrils, the same way it came in
Out through the mouth only

st.reveal: Dogs breathe out through side slits, so the outgoing air swirls backwards and even stirs up new scent towards the nostrils. That lets them sniff almost non-stop without blowing away the smell they are following.

A dog's nose can be wet or dry for many reasons, such as sleeping, the weather or licking. A dry nose alone is not a reliable sign of illness. If a dog seems unwell in other ways, a vet can check it.

sec.t:
When you breathe in, air and smells take the same path. A dog's nose is different. Inside, a fold of tissue splits the air in two. Most goes to the lungs. About an eighth goes to a special area at the back of the nose, packed with smell cells, where scent can build up.

When the dog breathes out, the air leaves through slits at the sides of the nose, swirling backwards. This lets the dog sniff in short bursts, up to about five times a second, without blowing away the smell it is following. A dog's wet nose also helps catch scent molecules.

Dogs work in police forces, armies and airports around the world. India's armed forces and police use breeds such as Labradors, German shepherds and Belgian Malinois to find explosives and drugs. At [[@airport-security|airports]], sniffer dogs can check hundreds of bags in the time a machine scans a few.

After earthquakes and building collapses, rescue dogs search for people trapped under rubble. Other dogs help farmers by sniffing out pests, or help scientists find animal droppings for wildlife studies.

Some dogs have been trained to smell illnesses. Dogs living with people who have diabetes can learn to warn them when their blood sugar drops too low. In studies, trained dogs have picked out samples from people with some cancers and with malaria.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, dogs at airports in Finland and the United Arab Emirates were trained to detect the virus by smell. Scientists are still testing how reliable this is. Dogs get tired and distracted, so researchers are also trying to build electronic noses that copy them.

Humans are not as bad at smelling as we think. We can tell apart thousands of different smells. In one experiment, people crawling on grass followed a chocolate scent trail by nose alone, a little like a dog, though much more slowly.

But a dog lives in a world of smell that we can barely picture. A walk around the block is like reading a newspaper full of messages left by other dogs. And every animal has its own superpower. For dogs it's smell. For the [[@power-mantis-shrimp|mantis shrimp]], it's eyes that see colours no human ever has. Your own nose has its own story too, which starts with [[@nose-smell|how smell works]].

text: The Sundarbans, shared by India and Bangladesh, is the world's largest mangrove forest.
Twice a day, tides flood the forest with salty water.
Mangroves protect the coast by slowing down storms and big waves.

Tigers live here by doing things most tigers rarely do. They swim across wide rivers, walk through sticky mud, catch fish and crabs, and drink salty water. They are the same Bengal tigers found in the rest of India, but they have learned to live in one of the hardest homes any big cat has.

spots: Sundarbans tigers swim between islands, sometimes several kilometres.
Mud has little air, so mangrove trees send up pencil-like roots to breathe.
Mangroves can live in salty water. Some push salt out through their leaves.

Salty or brackish river water, along with fresh water when they can find it

quiz.reveal: Sundarbans tigers drink the slightly salty water of the creeks and rivers, which most land animals avoid. They drink fresh water from rain-fed ponds when they can, and they also get some water from the animals they eat.

sec.t:
The Sundarbans grows at the mouth of three great rivers: the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna. Carrying mud all the way from the Himalayas, they built the largest delta on Earth. Where that mud meets the sea, hundreds of low islands are cut through by rivers and creeks.

Twice a day, as the [[@tides|tides]] rise, sea water pushes up the channels and floods much of the forest. As it falls, it uncovers mudflats full of crabs and mudskippers, fish that can hop about out of water. Some think the name comes from the *sundari*, a common mangrove tree here. Others say it means "beautiful forest" in [[@bengali-language|Bengali]].

There are about 100 tigers on the Indian side and more on the Bangladeshi side. Counting them is hard, because the tide washes away pawprints twice a day. Scientists use camera traps tied to trees and recognise each tiger by its [[@tiger-stripes|stripes]].

The tigers hunt chital deer and wild boar, but also fish, crabs and monitor lizards. They swim between islands, sometimes several kilometres. Because there is little fresh water, they drink the brackish creek water.

Millions of people live around the Sundarbans. Many fish, catch crabs or collect wild honey in the forest, and tiger attacks have long been a danger. In the 1980s, forest workers began wearing face masks on the backs of their heads, because tigers usually attack from behind. For a while the trick seemed to help.

Many people of the area, both Hindu and Muslim, honour Bonbibi, a forest goddess believed to protect those who enter the forest from tigers. Before going in, fishers and honey collectors often pray at her shrines.

Rising seas are a threat. Some low islands, such as Ghoramara, have been shrinking as the sea eats away their shores. Salt water is spreading further into fields and ponds. Scientists warn that [[@sea-level-rise|sea-level rise]] could drown parts of the forest unless the mangroves can build up mud fast enough to keep pace.

India's Sundarbans National Park became a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site in 1987, and Bangladesh's Sundarbans in 1997. Protecting it is a shared job for two countries, and the tigers swim across the border without needing a [[@passports|passport]].

text: Most cities take water from rivers, lakes or underground. [[@tap-water-pressure|Before it reaches your tap]], it passes through a treatment plant in several steps.

First, screens catch big things like sticks, leaves and plastic. Next, a chemical such as alum is stirred in. It makes tiny bits of mud stick together into larger clumps, which sink to the bottom of big settling tanks. The water then trickles through deep beds of sand and gravel, which trap smaller particles. Finally, it is disinfected, usually with chlorine, to kill any germs that remain. A little chlorine stays in the water to keep it safe all the way through the pipes to your home.

Each step removes something the last one missed. Along the way, workers test samples many times a day, checking for germs, cloudiness and the right amount of chlorine. If something looks wrong, they can stop the water before it leaves the plant.

It kills every germ instantly
It adds minerals to make the water taste better

st.reveal: Many particles in muddy water are too small and light to sink on their own. Alum makes them stick together into bigger, heavier clumps, called floc, that settle to the bottom of a tank. Families in India have long stirred a lump of alum, or phitkari, into water to clear it.

Stand it in a glass jar and slowly pour in muddy water. Compare the water before and after. It looks clearer, but don't drink it, because filters like this can't remove germs.
myth: If water looks clear, it's safe to drink.

Germs that cause diseases like cholera and typhoid are far too small to see. Clear water can still carry them, and murky water isn't always harmful. Only proper treatment, such as boiling or disinfection, makes water reliably safe.

sec.t:
Dirty water can carry tiny living things, such as bacteria, viruses and parasites. Some cause diseases like cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea, which can be very dangerous, especially for young children. The World Health Organization estimates that about 2 billion people around the world still lack safely managed [[@water-drink|drinking water]] at home.

Not all [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]] are harmful. Your gut is full of helpful ones. But the ones in sewage-polluted water can make people seriously ill. That's why water treatment has saved more lives than almost any other public health measure in history.

In 1908, Jersey City in New Jersey became the first US city to add chlorine to its drinking water continuously. Deaths from typhoid in American cities fell sharply over the following decades as others did the same. Chlorine is still the most common disinfectant in the world.

Some plants use ozone gas or strong ultraviolet light instead, which kill germs without leaving a taste. Ultraviolet light from the Sun works too. In some villages, people leave clear plastic bottles of water in strong sunlight for several hours to kill germs, a method recommended by health groups.

Many Indian homes treat their water again, even after it arrives from the city supply. [[@water-tech|Water purifiers]] with filters, ultraviolet lamps or reverse osmosis are common. Reverse osmosis pushes water through a very fine sheet that lets water through but stops most dissolved salts. It also wastes a lot of water, so it is best used where water really is salty or hard.

[[@boiling-water|Boiling]] is the oldest method of all. A minute at a rolling boil kills most germs. It doesn't remove chemicals or mud, but in an emergency it is one of the simplest ways to make water safer.

text: Bhajans and kirtans are kinds of devotional singing from India. A bhajan is a song of love and praise for God, usually short, tuneful and easy to join in. A kirtan is a gathering where people sing God's names or praises together, often in call and response: a leader sings a line and everyone sings it back.

Both grew out of the bhakti movement, a wave of devotion that spread across India from about the 7th century. [[bhakti|Bhakti]] poet-saints taught that anyone, rich or poor, high-born or low, could reach God through love and song, without needing priests or Sanskrit. Their songs are still sung in homes, temples, gurdwaras and festivals, and now in yoga studios from London to Los Angeles.

st.prompt: In a kirtan, what usually happens after the leader sings a line?

options.t: Everyone sings it back together
The audience claps once and stays silent
A different singer replies with a new verse

st.reveal: Most kirtan works by call and response. A lead singer sings a phrase, and the group repeats it. The tempo often starts slow and gets faster and louder, until it ends in a burst of sound or silence.

myth: Bhajans and kirtans belong only to one religion.

The words come mostly from Hindu traditions, but Sikh kirtan is central to worship in gurdwaras, Jains sing devotional songs called stavans, and Christian churches in India sing bhajans in Indian languages. Many styles overlap with Sufi music too.

sec.t:
Many of the best-loved bhajans were written centuries ago by poets who sang in the languages of ordinary people. Mirabai, a Rajput princess in the 1500s, gave up palace life to sing for Krishna. Kabir, a weaver from Varanasi, mocked empty rituals and sang of a God beyond any single religion. Surdas sang of Krishna's childhood, and Tulsidas retold the Ramayana in Awadhi.

The songs of [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai and Kabir]] are still sung by folk singers, classical stars and film playback singers alike.

In Maharashtra, Tukaram and Dnyaneshwar wrote songs called abhangs. Every year, lakhs of pilgrims walk to Pandharpur singing them, in a journey called the wari.

For Sikhs, kirtan means singing hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, the holy book. The Sikh Gurus wrote these hymns to be sung in particular ragas, and they are performed by trained musicians called ragis, usually with harmonium and tabla.

At the Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]], kirtan continues from early morning until late at night. Loudspeakers carry the music around the sacred pool, and the hymns are broadcast live on television and online.

During the freedom struggle, Mahatma Gandhi held prayer meetings with bhajans. His favourites included "Vaishnava Jana To", written by the Gujarati poet Narsinh Mehta in the 1400s, which describes a good person as one who feels the pain of others. Another, "Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram", was sung on the Salt March in 1930. Its familiar tune is usually credited to the musician Vishnu Digambar Paluskar. Both are still sung at schools and public events on 2 October.

In 1965, a monk named A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada arrived in the USA by cargo ship. In 1966, he began chanting under a tree in Tompkins Square Park in New York and founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, known as the Hare Krishna movement. Young Americans joined him.

The Beatles' George Harrison became a follower and produced a recording of the chant in 1969 that entered the British charts. Today, kirtan singers perform at festivals across America and Europe. Some singers in India now mix bhajans with rock guitars or electronic beats, while others keep to the old village tunes.

text: The Chipko movement was a protest by villagers in the Himalayan hills of today's [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]] in the 1970s. When logging companies came to cut their forests, people stood in the way, sometimes hugging the trees so they could not be felled. *Chipko* means "to stick to" in [[@hindi-language|Hindi]].
Most of the protesters were village women, who gathered firewood, fodder and water from the forest every day. They knew better than anyone what losing it would mean.
The movement became famous across India and the world. In 1980, the government banned cutting green trees in the region's hill forests for 15 years.

Soldiers from a nearby army camp

st.reveal: Most men of Reni were away when the loggers arrived. Gaura Devi gathered about 27 women and girls, and they stood in the forest refusing to move. After a tense standoff, the loggers left.

n.certNote: The main events are well recorded. People still debate who deserves most credit, since several leaders and many village women took part, and how often protesters literally hugged trees.

sec.t:
In the 1960s and early 1970s, the government sold the right to cut trees in the hills to companies from the plains. The timber went to cities and factories. Villagers were often not even allowed to cut a few trees for farm tools.

In 1970, a huge flood on the Alaknanda river swept away bridges, roads and villages. Many people blamed the bare, logged slopes, where nothing held the soil in place. Without roots, hillsides crumble in heavy rain, causing [[@floods-why|floods]] and [[@landslides|landslides]].

sec.h: The people who spread the word
sec.t:
Chipko had no single leader. A year before Reni, in 1973, Chandi Prasad Bhatt and his [[@cooperatives|village cooperative]] in Mandal had stopped a sports-goods company from felling ash trees. Bhatt later won the Ramon Magsaysay Award.

Sunderlal Bahuguna carried the message to Delhi. He met [[@indira-gandhi|Prime Minister Indira Gandhi]], and in 1980 her government brought in the logging ban. Then, between 1981 and 1983, he walked about 4,800 km across the Himalaya, village by village.

For a family in the hills, the forest was a kind of shop, pharmacy and water tank rolled into one. Oak and other broadleaf trees gave leaves to feed cows and goats, and fallen branches to cook with. Their roots soaked up rain and let it out slowly into springs.

Women did most of this work. They often walked for hours each day carrying loads of firewood and fodder on their heads. When forests shrank, the walks got longer. That is why women were at the front of Chipko. They were the first to feel the loss.

Chipko protesters also had a slogan. Roughly translated, it asked what the forest gives, and answered: soil, water and pure air. Many people across India still know it.

Chipko protesters often recalled a story from the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]]. In 1730, at Khejarli near Jodhpur, the Bishnoi community, whose faith forbids cutting green trees, refused to let a ruler's men fell their khejri trees. According to the tradition, Amrita Devi and 363 Bishnois gave their lives.

Chipko inspired the Appiko movement in Karnataka and protests in many other countries. In Kenya, [[@wangari-maathai|Wangari Maathai]] was building a tree-planting movement led by women at around the same time. Historians say Chipko showed that poor villagers could be some of the world's most determined environmentalists, because the forest was their home.

text: For most of history, old people were cared for by their children. They lived in the same house, shared the farm or the shop, and the younger generation took over the work. In much of India, that is still common.

But as people moved to cities and lived longer, many countries added other kinds of support. A pension is a regular payment to someone who has stopped working because of age. It might come from the government, from an employer or from savings built up over a working life. Societies also care for elders through health schemes, special housing, discounts on trains, and laws that protect them.

Many elderly Indians live alone or with just a spouse, especially when children move to cities or abroad. Surveys show that many older people, particularly widowed women, have little income of their own, which is why pensions and support schemes matter.

sec.t:
There are two main ways to fund pensions. In one, today's workers pay into a fund that is used to pay today's retirees. Social Security works mostly like this. In the other, each worker saves for their own old age, and the money grows over time through [[@money-interest-loans|interest]] and investments.

India's Employees' Provident Fund, started in 1952, works the second way. Each month, part of a worker's salary, plus a matching amount from the employer, goes into an account. Many government workers once received a guaranteed pension, but since 2004 most new central government staff join a savings-based system instead. Most Indian workers, though, have informal jobs with no employer pension at all. Since 2015, a scheme called Atal Pension Yojana has let them save small monthly amounts towards a fixed pension.

Large joint families have long been a safety net in India. [[@old-age-india|Grandparents]] help raise children, and children care for grandparents as they age. Many [[@families-world|families]] still live this way.

But more young Indians now move to other cities or countries for work. In 2007, Parliament passed a law that allows parents who cannot support themselves to claim maintenance from their adult children. The government also pays small monthly pensions to poor elderly people through the National Social Assistance Programme, started in 1995. Many states top this up.

Around the world, people are living longer and having fewer children. Japan has one of the oldest populations: almost three in ten people there are 65 or older. The country even has a public holiday, Respect for the Aged Day, every September.

India is younger, but that is changing. About one Indian in ten is now 60 or older, and that is expected to double to about one in five by 2050. A growing [[@population|population]] of elders means more need for [[@jobs-doctor|doctors who specialise in old age]], homes with [[@accessibility-tech|ramps]] and handrails, and pensions that keep pace with rising prices. How a country treats its oldest citizens tells you a lot about it.

text: A stock market is a place where people buy and sell shares in [[@global-companies|companies]]. A share is a tiny piece of a company. If a company is split into a crore shares and you own one, you own a crore-th of it.

Companies sell shares to raise money to grow, build factories or develop new products. After that, investors trade the shares with each other on a stock exchange. Prices go up when more people want to buy a share than sell it, and down when more want to sell. Today almost all of this happens on computers, in fractions of a second.

Buying a share makes you a part-owner. Unlike a lender, you are not promised your money back. If the company does well, your share can grow; if it fails, you can lose what you paid.

sec.t:
Selling shares is a way to share risk. In the 1600s, sending a ship to Asia for spices was hugely expensive and dangerous. Ships sank or were captured. So merchants pooled their money.

In 1602, the Dutch East India Company began selling shares to the public in Amsterdam. Anyone could buy a small part, and people traded these shares with each other. Many historians see this as the start of the modern stock market. Britain's [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], which later ruled much of India, was also owned by shareholders.

In the 1850s, a handful of brokers in Bombay began meeting under a [[@banyan|banyan tree]] near the Town Hall to trade shares. As the group grew, they moved from street to street. In 1875, they formed an association that became the Bombay Stock Exchange, the oldest in Asia. It now stands in a tall tower on Dalal Street in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]].

New York's story is similar. In 1792, 24 brokers signed an agreement under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street, setting rules for trading. That group became the New York Stock Exchange.

For a long time, trading meant brokers shouting and waving on a crowded floor. India's National Stock Exchange, set up in 1992, brought trading by computer screen to the whole country. Since 2020, the number of Indians with share-trading accounts has more than quadrupled, as buying shares on a phone app became easy.

{{story:east-india-company}}

A rising market is called a bull market, and a falling one a bear market. People say a bull attacks by tossing its horns up, while a bear swipes down.

To show how the whole market is doing, people use an index, an [[@averages|average]] of the prices of a group of big companies. India's best known are the Sensex, which tracks 30 companies on the BSE, and the Nifty 50 on the National Stock Exchange. In the USA, people follow the Dow Jones and the S&P 500.

Share prices can rise and fall sharply. In October 1929, the US stock market crashed, and the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]] followed. In 1992, India was shaken by a scandal in which a broker used money borrowed illegally from banks to push prices up.

After that scandal, India gave stronger powers to the Securities and Exchange Board of India, or SEBI, which polices the market. In the USA, a similar body, the Securities and Exchange Commission, was set up in 1934, after the 1929 crash.

Over many years, shares in good companies have usually grown more than money kept in a savings account, but there is no guarantee. Most experts advise putting money in for the long term, spreading it across many companies, and never investing money you might need soon.

text: An opinion poll asks a small group of people a question and uses their answers to estimate what a much bigger group thinks. Before an election, pollsters might phone or visit 1,000 to 2,000 voters and ask whom they plan to vote for.

The trick is choosing that small group well. If the [[sample|sample]] is picked at random, so that every kind of voter has a fair chance of being asked, the result usually lands close to the real answer. If it is picked carelessly, even millions of replies can mislead.

st.prompt: A pollster wants to know what all of India thinks. Roughly how many people does a good national poll need to ask?

options.t: About 1,000 to a few thousand, chosen at random
At least 1 crore people
Exactly one person from every village

st.reveal: The size of the sample matters much more than the size of the country. A random sample of about 1,000 people gives an answer that is usually within about 3 points of the truth. Asking more people helps, but less than you would think.

d.try: Put 30 red and 70 blue counters, beads or paper slips in a bag. Without looking, pull out 10, count the reds, and put them back. Do it five times. Your guesses will wobble around 3 reds out of 10, and the wobble is exactly what pollsters call the margin of error.
myth: To know what a country thinks, you have to ask a large part of the country.
What matters most is that the people asked are chosen fairly, so every group has a fair chance of being included. A huge but lopsided sample can be far worse than a small, random one.

sec.t:
Think of a big pot of dal. You don't need to drink the whole pot to know if it needs salt. One spoonful is enough, as long as the dal has been stirred well.

A poll works the same way. Random sampling is the stirring. It makes sure the spoonful holds a little of everything: young and old, city and village, rich and poor. That is why a poll of 1,000 people can work for a country as big as India. The size of the pot hardly matters. What matters is the stir.

sec.h: The poll that got it wrong

sec.t:
Every poll comes with a margin of error. For a random sample of 1,000 people, it is about 3 percentage points. So if a poll says 52% support a candidate, the true figure is probably somewhere between 49% and 55%.

That is why a close race is so hard to call. If two candidates are 2 points apart, the poll can't really say who is ahead. Pollsters also adjust, or "weight", their results. If too few young people answered, each young person's answer counts a little more, so the sample matches the population. This part of the work is based on [[@probability|probability]], and it is where good and bad polls often differ.

An exit poll asks people how they voted just after they leave the polling station. In India, the [[@election-commission|Election Commission]] does not allow exit poll results to be published until the last phase of voting is over, so that they can't sway people still waiting to vote. In the USA, TV networks usually wait until polls close in a state before reporting.

Exit polls are not always right. In India's 2024 general election, most exit polls predicted a much larger win for the ruling alliance than it actually got. In the USA in 2016, several state polls underestimated support for Donald Trump.

[[@vote-how|Elections]] are just one use for polls. Governments, scientists and companies use the same methods to find out how many children have been vaccinated, what people think of a new law or which snack flavour to sell. A good [[@surveys|survey]] asks clear questions in a fair order. A question like "Don't you agree that homework is too long?" pushes people towards one answer, and a careful pollster would never ask it that way. Even the order of questions matters. Ask about crime first, and people may rate their police differently on the next question.

text: A parade is a crowd of people moving along a route in an organised line, usually with music, flags, costumes or vehicles, while others watch. Countries, cities and communities hold parades to celebrate, to remember, to give thanks, to worship and to show strength.

A national parade, like India's Republic Day parade in New Delhi, tells a story about the whole country. Its soldiers, states, culture and history all pass by in a couple of hours. A street parade on a festival can do the same for a single town or community. In both, the point is that people gather in one place and share the same moment.

st.prompt: In 1950, India's first Republic Day parade was not held on Rajpath. Where was it?

At the Red Fort
In Mumbai, at the Gateway of India

st.reveal: The first parade, in 1950, was held at Irwin Stadium, now the Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium. For a few years it moved between different venues, then settled on Rajpath in 1955. That road was renamed Kartavya Path in 2022.

Independence came on 15 August 1947. Republic Day, 26 January, marks the day in 1950 when India's Constitution came into force and the country became a republic. Independence Day is marked mainly with a flag-raising and a speech at the Red Fort.

sec.t:
Some of the oldest parades were about power. In [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]], a general who won a great war could be granted a "triumph". He rode through the city in [[@wheel-to-chariot|a chariot]], followed by soldiers, captured treasure and prisoners, while crowds cheered.

Many countries still hold military parades. Tanks roll by, soldiers march in step and jets fly overhead. These parades are meant to make citizens feel proud and safe. They also send a message to other countries about a nation's strength. Some people think military parades are a fine tradition, while others feel they cost too much or glorify war.

Religious processions are parades too, and some are among the largest gatherings on Earth. In the town of Puri in [[@odisha|Odisha]], the Rath Yatra takes place every summer. Images of Lord Jagannath and his brother and sister are placed on three towering wooden chariots, built new each year. Huge crowds pull them through the streets with thick ropes.

European travellers who saw the festival centuries ago were amazed by the size of the chariots. Their accounts gave English the word "juggernaut", for something enormous that seems impossible to stop.

In the USA, parades are often about fun. The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in [[@new-york|New York]] began in 1924. From 1927, it added huge balloons shaped like cartoon characters. Today they can be as tall as a five-storey building, held down by dozens of handlers each.

In Pasadena, California, the Rose Parade has run on New Year's Day since 1890. Every surface of each float must be covered with flowers, seeds, bark or other plants. New York's St Patrick's Day parade, honouring Irish heritage, is even older. Irish soldiers first marched in 1762.

Some parades are quiet. On Remembrance Day and Veterans Day, old soldiers march to honour people who died in wars. Victory parades welcome sports teams home. When India's cricket team won the T20 World Cup in 2024, crowds packed Mumbai's Marine Drive to cheer an open-top bus.

People also march to ask for change. In 1930, Gandhi and his followers walked to Dandi in the Salt March, and in 1963, about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington in the USA. These weren't parades in the festive sense, but they used the same idea: when many people move together in public, everyone notices.

text: Footballers bend the ball by making it spin. A player strikes it off-centre, often with the inside or outside of the foot, so it leaves the boot rotating as well as flying forward.

As the spinning ball moves, it drags a thin layer of air around with it. On one side, the spin moves with the passing air. On the other side, it moves against it. That makes the air flow off the back of the ball at an angle, and the ball gets pushed the other way. This sideways push is called the Magnus effect, after a German scientist who studied it in 1852.

st.prompt: A right-footed player strikes the right-hand side of the ball with the inside of the foot. Which way will it curve?

options.t: From right to left
From left to right
Straight, then it dips

st.reveal: Striking off-centre makes the ball spin. Air gets dragged around faster on one side, and the ball is pushed towards the side spinning away from the direction of travel. Inside-foot shots from a right-footer usually curl right to left.

src: Dupeux, G. et al. (2010), The spinning ball spiral, New Journal of Physics.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Magnus effect.

myth: A curling ball bends only because the wind pushes it.
Wind can help, but footballers curve the ball indoors too. The bend comes from spin, which makes the air push harder on one side of the ball than the other.

sec.h: The free kick that broke physics
sec.t:
On 3 June 1997, Brazil played France in a warm-up tournament in Lyon. Brazil's left-back, Roberto Carlos, placed the ball about 35 metres from goal. He ran up and struck it with the outside of his left foot.

The ball flew well wide of the wall, so far that a ball boy near the corner flag flinched. Then it hooked sharply back and went in off the post. The French goalkeeper barely moved.

For years, people called it impossible. In 2010, French physicists worked out why it wasn't. A spinning ball's curve gets tighter as it slows down, so its path becomes a spiral. Carlos hit it so hard and so far that the spiral had time to show.

Some players do the opposite. They hit the ball with the hard top of the foot, right through the centre, with almost no spin. This is a knuckleball.

Without spin, the air flowing around the ball can't settle into a steady pattern. Small bumps and seams make it break away first on one side, then the other. The ball wobbles and dips unpredictably, like a leaf in a breeze. Cristiano Ronaldo became famous for these shots. Even the kicker doesn't know exactly where it will go.

Older footballs had 32 stitched leather panels. Modern balls have fewer, smoother panels that are glued together. Each change alters how air grips the surface.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, many goalkeepers complained that the new ball, the Jabulani, swerved strangely. Wind-tunnel tests later suggested its smooth surface made it more likely to wobble at the speeds of long shots. Ball makers now add tiny grooves and textures, a bit like the dimples on a golf ball, to make flight more predictable.

Spin bends balls in nearly every sport. A baseball pitcher's curveball, a table tennis topspin smash and a tennis serve all use the Magnus effect. [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] described curving tennis balls in 1672, long before anyone filmed football.

Cricket is the odd one out. A fast bowler's swing usually comes from the shiny and rough halves of the ball and the angle of the seam, not from spin. It is a different trick with the same air, and it's why [[@cricket-swing|cricket swing]] puzzles even scientists.

Coaches teach young players to strike the ball low and to the side, wrapping the foot around it, and to follow through across the body. The 2002 film *Bend It Like Beckham*, about a British Indian girl who wants to play football, took its name from this skill.

Practice turns physics into feel. Top players rarely think about air pressure. They just know where the ball will end up, the same way a spin bowler knows how much a ball will [[@cricket-spin|turn]] before it lands.

text: Your gut, especially the large intestine, is home to tens of trillions of [[microbe|microbes]], mostly bacteria. Scientists call this community the gut microbiome.

These bacteria live off the parts of your food that your own body can't break down, such as the tough fibre in vegetables, dal and whole grains. In return they make useful substances, including vitamin K, which helps blood clot, and chemicals that feed the cells lining your gut. They also help teach your [[@immune-system|immune system]] which microbes are friends and which are enemies, and they take up space that harmful germs might otherwise grab.

st.prompt: For years, books said bacteria in your body outnumber your own cells by 10 to 1. What did a careful recount in 2016 find?

options.t: About 1 to 1, roughly equal numbers
Bacteria are only a tiny fraction

st.reveal: Scientists in Israel and Canada recounted and found about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells. The old 10-to-1 figure came from a rough guess made in the 1970s that kept being repeated.

Only a small number of kinds of bacteria cause disease. Most bacteria in your gut are harmless or helpful, and you would struggle to stay healthy without them.

sec.t:
Each person carries hundreds of different kinds of bacteria, and no two people have exactly the same mix. Most live in the colon, the last wide part of the gut, where food moves slowly and there is almost no oxygen. Your stomach, full of strong acid, holds very few.

All together, your gut bacteria weigh only about 0.2 kg, roughly as much as a cup of uncooked rice. Yet some estimates suggest they carry far more genes than your own cells do.

Nobody knew any of this until the 1670s, when the Dutch cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek peered through tiny lenses he had ground himself. These early [[@microscopes|microscopes]] showed him "little animals" swimming in pond water and in the gunk scraped from his own teeth. They were bacteria, seen for the first time.

sec.h: Where your first bacteria come from
sec.t:
Before birth, a baby's gut has few or no bacteria. During birth and the first days of life, babies pick them up from their mother, from milk, from skin and from the world around them. Breast milk even contains special sugars the baby can't digest, which feed helpful bacteria instead.

By about the age of three, a child's gut community looks much like an adult's. It keeps changing with food, illness and medicine.

[[@antibiotics|Antibiotics]] kill harmful bacteria, which can save lives. But they also kill many helpful ones, which is why some people get an upset stomach while taking them. The gut community usually recovers over the following weeks.

Foods like [[@curd-yogurt|curd and yogurt]] contain live bacteria. Scientists are still studying how much they help, since most of these bacteria pass through rather than settling down.

The gut microbiome is one of the busiest areas of medical research today. In the USA, the National Institutes of Health ran the Human Microbiome Project from 2007 to 2016 to map these communities.

Some studies, many in mice, hint that gut bacteria may affect weight, allergies and even mood. These links are interesting but not yet proven in people. Be wary of products that promise big health changes from a pill of bacteria. If you have tummy troubles that keep coming back, a doctor is the person to ask.

text: No. The idea of five senses (sight, hearing, [[@nose-smell|smell]], taste and touch) comes from the ancient Greek thinker Aristotle. It is easy to remember, but it leaves a lot out.

Scientists define a sense as a way of detecting something using special [[sensor|sensors]] called receptors. By that measure, you also have a [[@motion-sickness|sense of balance]], a sense of where your arms and legs are, a sense of hot and cold, and a sense of [[@pain|pain]]. You can feel hunger, thirst and a full bladder. Some lists reach more than 20.
The exact number depends on how you count. What is clear is that five is too few.

st.prompt: Which sense tells you that you're spinning, even with your eyes closed?

options.t: Your sense of balance, from fluid moving in your inner ear
Your sense of touch, from air on your skin
Your sense of hearing

st.reveal: Deep in each ear are three tiny looped tubes filled with fluid. When you spin, the fluid swirls and bends tiny hairs, sending signals to your brain. When you stop, the fluid keeps swirling a moment, which is why you feel dizzy.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sense.
Cole J. (1995) Pride and a Daily Marathon. MIT Press.
n.certNote: Scientists agree humans have more than five senses, but they don't agree on the exact number. Depending on how you count, lists range from about nine to more than twenty.

d.try: Bend a paper clip into a U shape with the two ends about 1 centimetre apart. With a friend's eyes closed, gently touch either one end or both ends to their fingertip, then to their arm, and ask "one or two?" Fingertips can usually tell, but on the arm two points often feel like one.
myth: Humans have exactly five senses.
The list of five goes back to Aristotle, over 2,300 years ago. Scientists now count many more, including balance, temperature, pain and the sense of where your body parts are.

sec.t:
Close your eyes and touch your nose with your finger. You can do it because of proprioception, the sense of where your body parts are and how they're moving. Sensors in your muscles, tendons and joints keep reporting to your brain, all day, without you noticing.

Ian Waterman, from England, lost this sense at the age of 19 after a rare illness damaged his nerves. He could still feel pain and temperature, but he could no longer tell where his limbs were without looking. Doctors expected him never to walk again. By watching his body and thinking about every movement, he taught himself to walk, write and drive. The scientist Jonathan Cole wrote a book about him.

Your sense of balance comes from the inner ear, right next to the part that handles hearing. It contains three tiny curved tubes filled with fluid, set at different angles, plus small sacs with crystals that sense gravity and speed.

This system works with your eyes and your body-position sense to keep you steady. When they disagree, for instance reading in a moving car, you can feel sick.

Your skin holds separate receptors for different jobs. Some respond to light touch, some to pressure, some to vibration. Others respond to warmth or to cold. Pain receptors respond to damage or the threat of it.

Chilli peppers trick your heat receptors. The chemical capsaicin switches on the same sensors that react to heat, which is why a hot curry feels hot. Mint does the opposite, triggering cold sensors.

Inside your body, more sensors track your blood pressure, oxygen levels and stomach stretch. This inner sensing helps explain feelings like hunger or a racing heart.

sec.h: Senses that animals have and we don't
A brain that blends it all
sec.t:
Your brain doesn't treat senses separately. It mixes them. Much of what you call taste is really smell, which is why food tastes dull when you have a cold. What [[@eyes-see|your eyes see]] can change what you think you hear.

Some people experience synaesthesia, where one sense triggers another. They might see colours when they hear music, or feel that each number has its own colour. For them, it is a normal part of how the world feels.

text: Your body works best at about 37 °C. When you get hot, from running, from a fever or from a summer afternoon, your brain switches on millions of tiny sweat glands in your [[@skin|skin]]. Each one is a coiled tube that pumps out water with a little [[@salt|salt]].

Sweat itself doesn't cool you. What cools you is sweat turning into vapour and floating away. Changing from liquid to gas takes heat, and that heat is pulled from your skin. It's the same reason a wet cloth on your forehead feels cool, or why a clay pot, a matka, [[@how-fridges-cold|keeps water cool]] as it slowly seeps and evaporates from the outside.

st.prompt: It's 35 °C in both Delhi in May and Mumbai in July. In which city does sweating cool you down better?

options.t: Dry Delhi, because sweat evaporates faster in dry air
Humid Mumbai, because there's more water around

st.reveal: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates. In dry air it disappears quickly and carries heat away. In very humid air, the air is already full of water, so sweat just drips off and you stay hot and sticky.

sec.t:
Most of your sweat glands are the small kind, spread over almost your whole body. They are packed most tightly on your palms, the soles of your feet and your forehead. They make thin, watery sweat for cooling.

The second kind lives mainly in your armpits and groin. These glands start working at [[@puberty-basics|puberty]]. Their sweat is thicker and contains fats and proteins. Fresh, it has hardly any smell. But [[bacteria|bacteria]] living on the skin feed on it and give off smelly substances. That's what body odour is, and why washing and clean clothes make such a difference.

Sweat only works if it can evaporate. On a dry, [[@heat-body|hot day]] in Rajasthan or Arizona, sweat vanishes almost as soon as it appears, and you may not even feel wet. On a humid monsoon day in Mumbai, Kolkata or Chennai, or a summer day in Florida, the air is already full of water. Sweat can't escape, so it drips off, and you stay hot.

That's why humid heat feels worse than dry heat at the same temperature, and why it can be more dangerous. Weather forecasters use a heat index to describe how hot it really feels. In very [[@hot-places|hot places]], the most important thing is to drink plenty of [[@water-drink|water]] and rest in the shade.

Palms often get damp before a test or a stage show. That's emotional sweating. When you're nervous, the same alarm system that speeds up your heart switches on the sweat glands in your palms, soles and armpits, even if you aren't hot.

Scientists think sweaty palms may once have helped our ancestors grip branches or tools better when in danger. Today it mostly just makes holding a pen tricky. Some people sweat much more than others, and a small number sweat so much that it gets in the way of daily life. Doctors can help with that.

text: Tuberculosis, or TB, is an infection caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It usually attacks the [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]], but it can affect other parts of the body too. People with TB in their lungs can spread it when they cough, sneeze or even talk, sending tiny droplets into the air.

Most people who breathe in the germ never get sick, because their immune system walls it off. But if the immune system is weakened, the germs can wake up and cause disease. TB can be cured with a course of [[@antibiotics|antibiotics]] lasting about six months. India has more TB cases than any other country, about a quarter of the world's total, which is why the disease matters so much there.

About one week
The rest of the patient's life

st.reveal: Ordinary TB is usually cured with about six months of daily antibiotics. Patients often feel better after a few weeks, but stopping early can let the germs come back stronger and resistant to the medicines.

myth: TB is a disease of the past that only happens to poor people.

TB is still one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases, and anyone can catch it because it spreads through the air. It does hit hardest where people are crowded, underfed or have other illnesses, and it is curable with treatment.

sec.t:
TB has been with humans for thousands of years. Signs of it have been found in [[@myths-egyptian|ancient Egyptian mummies]]. In the 1800s it was so common in Europe and America that it was called "the white plague". It was also known as consumption, because it seemed to eat people away. The English poet John Keats died of it in 1821, aged 25.

Nobody knew the cause until 1882. On 24 March that year, the German doctor Robert Koch announced he had found the bacterium, using careful staining and [[@microscopes|microscopes]]. That date is now World TB Day.

Before medicines, patients were often sent to sanatoriums, special hospitals in the hills where they rested in fresh air for months. In 1956, doctors at the Tuberculosis Chemotherapy Centre in Madras, now Chennai, ran a famous study. They compared patients treated in a sanatorium with patients who took their medicines at home.

Both groups did about equally well, and family members at home were not put at extra risk once treatment began. The study changed TB care around the world, showing that patients could be treated at home if they took their medicines regularly.

According to the WHO, about 10.8 million people worldwide fell ill with TB in 2023, and about 1.25 million died. India accounted for around a quarter of the cases. Crowded homes, undernourishment, diabetes and smoking all raise the risk of the disease becoming active.

India's National TB Elimination Programme offers free testing and treatment, tracks patients through a system called Nikshay, and gives money for nutrition during treatment. The government set a goal of ending TB well ahead of the United Nations' [[@sustainable-goals|2030 target]]. Cases and deaths have fallen, but the disease is far from gone.

Most babies born in India get the BCG vaccine soon after birth. It was developed in France and first used in 1921. BCG protects young children well against the most severe forms of TB, but it works less well in adults. Scientists are testing new TB vaccines, and there's no shame in having TB. It's an infection like any other, and getting tested and treated protects your family too.

text: Digital maps learn about traffic mostly from phones. When people allow it, their phones quietly send small, anonymous updates about where they are and how fast they're moving. If hundreds of phones on one road are moving at walking pace, the map knows there is a jam and paints that road red. If they're zipping along, it turns green.

The map company also mixes in other clues. Some cities have road sensors, drivers report accidents, and there are years of records about how busy each road usually gets at that hour. A computer combines all this to guess your travel time and pick the fastest route.

st.prompt: How does a map app know that a road is jammed right now?

options.t: Phones on that road report that they are moving slowly

sec.t:
Before a map can say anything about traffic, your phone must know where it is. It listens to signals from [[@satellites-help|satellites]] orbiting about 20,000 km above Earth. The best-known system is [[@gps-how|GPS]], run by the United States, with about 30 satellites.

Each satellite constantly broadcasts the exact time and its position. Your phone compares signals from at least four satellites. Because the signals take slightly different times to arrive, the phone can work out its distance from each one and pinpoint its own spot, often to within a few metres. That spot is described by two numbers, latitude and longitude, called [[@coordinates|coordinates]].

India has its own regional system, [[@navic|NavIC]], run by ISRO, with satellites that cover India and the area around it. Many phones sold in India can now use it alongside GPS.

Speed is the key traffic clue. A single phone crawling along could just be someone walking, or a bus stopping. But if many phones on the same stretch of road all slow down, something is going on.

Map apps also learn the rhythm of a city. They can learn that a big road in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] clogs around 9 a.m. on weekdays, or that roads near a stadium fill up after a cricket match. By mixing live reports with patterns from the past, they predict how traffic will look by the time you reach each road.

Some apps, like Waze, also ask drivers to report things directly: a crash, a pothole, a car stopped on the shoulder.

{{story:coordinates}}

In February 2020, a Berlin artist named Simon Weckert put 99 second-hand phones, all running Google Maps, into a small red handcart. He walked slowly up and down quiet streets. On the map, the empty roads turned red, and some drivers were told to avoid them.

His project showed how much the map trusts phones. Real traffic data is far messier than one cart, and map companies mix many sources to catch mistakes. Still, it was a playful reminder that maps are clever guesses, not perfect pictures.

Once the map knows the traffic, it must pick a route. A city has millions of possible paths between two points. The app uses [[@algorithms|algorithms]], step-by-step methods, to search them efficiently, adding up the expected time on each road segment.

It also keeps updating as you drive. If a jam builds ahead, it may suggest a new route. Delivery companies, taxi apps and ambulances all depend on this. Even [[@self-driving|self-driving cars]] use detailed digital maps, though for steering they rely on their own sensors more than on traffic reports.

text: Chittorgarh is one of the largest forts in India. It sits on a flat-topped hill about 180 metres above the plains of southern Rajasthan. Its walls wind for kilometres around palaces, temples, towers and water tanks. The whole fort covers about 700 acres, about as much ground as 400 football fields.

For centuries it was the capital of Mewar, a kingdom ruled by Rajput kings called the Ranas. Chittorgarh was besieged and captured three times, in 1303, 1535 and 1568. Each time, the stories of what happened became legends told across India.
Since 2013 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

st.reveal: Rana Udai Singh II had founded Udaipur in 1559, in hills that were easier to defend. After Akbar captured Chittorgarh, Udaipur became the new capital of Mewar.

d.try: Draw a map of an imaginary hill fort. Mark where you would put the gates, the water tanks and the watchtowers, and think about why each goes where it does. Water was the biggest worry during a long siege.
myth: The story of Rani Padmini and Alauddin Khalji is proven history.

Alauddin Khalji really did capture Chittorgarh in 1303. But the tale of Padmini comes mainly from the poem Padmavat, written by Malik Muhammad Jayasi in 1540. Many historians think she may be a legend, while others believe the story holds a memory of real events.
