sec.t:
Tradition says a local ruler built the first fort here in the 600s. Later, the Guhila and Sisodia families of [[@rajputs|Rajputs]] made it their stronghold. To reach the top, you climb a zig-zag road through seven gates, each built to slow down an attacking army.

Inside the walls stood a whole town, with homes, markets and temples, so thousands of people could hold out for months. Water was the key to surviving a siege. Tradition says the fort once had 84 water bodies, though only about 22 remain. Rainwater ran into tanks and step wells. One famous reservoir, Gaumukh, is fed by a spring that trickles out of a rock carved like a cow's mouth.

In 1303, Alauddin Khalji, sultan of Delhi, besieged the fort for months and captured it. In 1535, Bahadur Shah, the sultan of Gujarat, took it. And in 1567–68 the Mughal emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] besieged it for about four months before it fell.

Chronicles and legends say that during these sieges, the women of the fort chose to die in fire rather than be captured. This practice was called jauhar. The men then rode out to fight to the end. People in Rajasthan remember these events as both brave and deeply sad.

After 1568, Mewar's rulers moved their capital to Udaipur. The Rana Maharana Pratap, who kept fighting the Mughals for years, never got Chittorgarh back.

{{story:knights-castles}}

Two stone towers rise above the fort. The Vijay Stambh, or Victory Tower, was built by Rana Kumbha to celebrate a victory over the sultan of Malwa. Finished in 1448, it is about 37 metres tall, with nine storeys covered in carvings of gods and goddesses. You can climb a narrow staircase of about 157 steps inside it to the top, where small windows look out over the town below. Its walls carry so many carved figures that it is sometimes called a dictionary of Hindu sculpture.

Rana Kumbha also built or rebuilt many of the fort's walls and temples. The older Kirti Stambh, or Tower of Fame, was built by a Jain merchant, probably in the 1100s. It is about 22 metres tall and is dedicated to Adinatha, the first Jain tirthankara.

Chittorgarh is full of stories. The poet-saint Mirabai lived here as a royal bride in the early 1500s. She was famous for singing to Krishna instead of living like a princess, and her songs are still sung today, as you can read in [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai and Kabir]].

The best-known legend is that of Rani Padmini, a queen said to be so beautiful that Alauddin Khalji attacked the fort to win her. It comes from a poem written in 1540, long after the siege. Historians still debate whether she was real.

And the strangest part? Chittorgarh is just one of a whole chain of giant hill forts, some with walls long enough to be seen from far away, as you can find in [[@rajasthan-forts|Rajasthan's forts]].

text: At the end of the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], a few European countries still ruled huge parts of Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific. Britain, France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Portugal had colonies on almost every continent.

Over the next 30 years, nearly all of those colonies became independent nations. People in the colonies had been demanding freedom for decades, and the war had left the old empires poorer and weaker. This great change is called decolonisation. It added more than 80 new countries to the [[@united-nations|United Nations]].

options.t: About one in a hundred

Close to one in three

st.reveal: The United Nations says that when it was founded, about 750 million people, nearly a third of the world's population, lived in territories that depended on colonial powers. Today only about 2 million do.

d.try: Look at a world map or atlas and pick five countries in Africa or Asia. Find out the year each became independent and who ruled it before. Colour each one on a blank map according to the decade it became free and look for patterns.
myth: Colonial powers gave their colonies freedom as a gift.

A few handovers were peaceful and planned, but almost all followed years of protest, organising and sometimes war by people in the colonies. Empires let go mostly because holding on had become too costly.

sec.t:
The war cost Britain and France enormous sums, and Japan's early victories in Asia had shown that European armies could be beaten. Millions of soldiers from the colonies, including about 2.5 million from India, had fought for the Allies. They came home asking why they should fight for freedom abroad but not have it at home.

The new United Nations Charter spoke of the "self-determination of peoples", meaning their right to choose their own government. The two new superpowers, the USA and the Soviet Union, disagreed about most things, but both opposed the old European empires.

In 1957 Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became one of the first colonies in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence. At midnight on the big day, Nkrumah told a huge crowd in Accra that Ghana was "free for ever".

Then came 1960, when 17 African nations became independent, including [[@nigeria|Nigeria]], Senegal and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Some handovers were peaceful. Others came only after bitter wars, such as Algeria's eight-year fight against France and the Mau Mau uprising in Kenya. Portugal held on to its African colonies until the mid-1970s.

Each new nation had to design a flag, write an anthem, print money and train its own officials. Ghana chose red, gold and green, the colours of Ethiopia's flag. Ethiopia had kept its independence for nearly all of the colonial era, and many African countries later borrowed its colours as a sign of shared freedom.

Many new nations did not want to pick a side in the [[@cold-war|Cold War]]. In 1955 leaders from 29 Asian and African countries met at Bandung in Indonesia to talk about cooperation. [[@nehru|Nehru]], China's Zhou Enlai and Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser were among them. In 1961 the Non-Aligned Movement was founded, with India's Jawaharlal Nehru among its leading voices, alongside leaders from Egypt, Yugoslavia, Indonesia and Ghana.

Freedom brought hard problems too. Many borders had been drawn by colonial officials with rulers on maps, cutting across communities, languages and rivers. That left some new countries with disputes and conflicts that still continue.

Some places changed hands much later. India took [[@goa-liberation|Goa]] from Portugal in 1961, and Britain and Portugal handed Hong Kong and Macau to China in 1997 and 1999. A handful of small territories around the world are still governed from far away, and the United Nations keeps a list of them.

text: For most of history, medicine meant herbs, rest, prayer and a few brave operations. Healers in Egypt, India, China and Greece wrote careful notes about illnesses and remedies, and some of their cures worked. But nobody knew that tiny living things called germs caused many diseases.

Most of the huge changes are less than 250 years old. Vaccines arrived in 1796. Painless surgery came in the 1840s, and clean operating rooms soon after. Germs were identified in the late 1800s, and [[@antibiotics|antibiotics]] followed in the 1940s. Together these changes more than doubled how long the average person lives.

st.reveal: Without a safe way to put people to sleep, speed was everything. Some surgeons could remove a leg in a few minutes. Strong drinks and opium helped a little, but most patients felt the pain until ether and chloroform arrived in the 1840s.

Ask an older relative what medicines or treatments they remember changing in their lifetime.
myth: Doctors have always washed their hands and cleaned their tools before treating patients.

Clean hands and tools only became normal in the late 1800s. In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that handwashing saved mothers' lives in a Vienna hospital, but many doctors refused to believe him at first.

sec.t:
Ancient doctors were careful observers. An Egyptian scroll from about 3,600 years ago describes how to treat broken bones and wounds. In India, the Sushruta Samhita, written down well over 1,500 years ago (experts disagree on the exact date), describes more than a hundred surgical tools. It explains how to remove cloudy lenses from eyes and rebuild a damaged nose with skin from the cheek, an early kind of plastic surgery linked to the healer [[@sushruta|Sushruta]].

In Greece, Hippocrates and his followers taught that illness had natural causes, not angry gods. In Persia, Ibn Sina finished his Canon of Medicine in about 1025. Students in Europe and the Middle East used it for about 600 years. In India, the Charaka Samhita laid out ideas about diet, digestion and daily habits that are still part of Ayurveda.

Many old ideas were wrong. In Europe, doctors believed the body held four fluids, or humours, that had to stay in balance. To fix an "excess" of blood, they cut patients and let them bleed. When George Washington fell ill in 1799, his doctors drained a large amount of his blood. He died within a day.

Surgery was terrifying. With no way to stop pain, the best surgeons were the fastest. Wounds often became infected afterwards, because no one cleaned their hands or tools. Hospitals could be dirty, crowded places. Florence Nightingale's work with wounded soldiers in the 1850s helped turn nursing into a trained profession and made cleanliness a hospital rule.

In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner scratched material from a cowpox sore into a boy's arm. The boy became protected against smallpox. This was the first [[@vaccines|vaccine]], and it led to smallpox being wiped out worldwide in 1980.

In 1846, a dentist in Boston put a patient to sleep with ether gas during a public operation. The patient felt nothing, and the news spread around the world within months. In 1867, the British surgeon Joseph Lister began using carbolic acid to kill germs on wounds and tools, and far fewer of his patients died from infections.

Microscopes helped scientists like Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch prove that germs cause disease. In 1897, Ronald Ross, working in Secunderabad, showed that mosquitoes spread malaria. He won a Nobel Prize for it in 1902.

{{story:microscopes}}

In 1895, X-rays let doctors see bones without cutting. In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria on one of his dishes. That mould gave us penicillin, which by the 1940s was saving soldiers and children alike.

Since then, medicine has added blood transfusions, heart surgery, organ transplants and scans that show the brain at work. India was declared free of polio in 2014, after years of vaccination drives that reached every village. Doctors still make mistakes, and new diseases still appear. But a child born today, in India or the USA, can expect to live more than twice as long as a child born in 1900.

text: The first person to fly across the United States was Calbraith Perry Rodgers, a tall, cigar-chewing pilot known as Cal. He left Sheepshead Bay in Brooklyn, New York, on 17 September 1911. He reached Pasadena, California, on 5 November, 49 days later.

He did not fly straight. He hopped from field to field, landing about 70 times, and crashed so often that mechanics rebuilt much of the plane on the way. His time actually in the air was only about 82 hours. Today a passenger jet does the same trip in about six hours, while you watch a film and eat peanuts.

myth: The first flight across America was a single, non-stop dash.
The first crossing in 1911 took 49 days and about 70 stops. Nobody crossed without landing until 1923, when two army pilots flew a Fokker T-2 from New York to San Diego.

sec.h: A prize, a plane and a grape soda
sec.t:
In 1910 the newspaper owner William Randolph Hearst offered $50,000 to the first pilot to cross the country in 30 days or less. Rodgers had learned to fly only that summer, at the school run by the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]]. He bought one of their light Model EX planes.

Planes were costly, so he found a sponsor. A company selling a new grape soda called Vin Fiz paid him for every mile flown, as long as the drink's name was painted on the wings. The plane became a flying advertisement, years before most people had ever seen a plane at all.

sec.h: A train full of spare parts

sec.t:
The 30 days ran out while Rodgers was still in Texas, so he never won Hearst's money. He kept going anyway, because being first still mattered to him. His winding route through Chicago and the southern deserts covered about 6,800 km, far longer than a straight line.

After Pasadena he wanted to touch the ocean too. A crash delayed him for weeks, but on 10 December 1911 he rolled his wheels into the Pacific surf at Long Beach. That same year, on the other side of the world, a small plane carried the first airmail in [[@hist-first-flight-india|India]], across the Yamuna at Allahabad.

Records fell quickly after that. In 1921 the US Post Office flew mail coast to coast in relays, partly at night, in about 33 hours. In May 1923 two army pilots, Oakley Kelly and John Macready, flew a big Fokker T-2 from New York to San Diego without landing once. It took them about 27 hours.

The most startling record came in 1990. A Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane crossed from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C. in a little over an hour. That is less time than many school buses take to finish their morning round.

sec.h: Where the Vin Fiz is now
sec.t:
The patched-up Vin Fiz survived. It hangs today in the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]] National Air and Space Museum in Washington. Next to the sleek jets around it, it looks like a kite made of wood, wire and cloth.

Rodgers himself died in a crash at Long Beach in April 1912, only months after his big flight. His trip proved something people doubted in 1911: a plane could link one coast to the other. The question of how a machine of wood and cloth stays up at all is answered by the same [[@airplanes-fly|physics that lifts every airliner]] today.

text: People keep diaries to remember their lives, sort out their feelings and record things they think matter. A diary is a private space. You can be honest there in a way you might not be with anyone else.

Some diaries turn into history. Because diarists write things down as they happen, their pages show what ordinary days were like, long after everyone involved has gone. A boy's worries about exams in 1890 or a girl's notes during a war can tell historians more than an official report.

sec.t:
The word diary comes from the Latin *dies*, meaning day. Many people write a few lines each evening: what they did, who they met, what made them laugh or angry. Others write only when something big happens.

Diaries help [[@memory|memory]]. Most of what happens to us fades within weeks. Reading an old diary can bring back the smell of a classroom or the taste of a holiday meal you'd forgotten. Some scientists have also found that writing about worries can help people feel calmer, though not everyone finds it useful.

sec.h: The man who buried his cheese

sec.t:
Anne Frank was a Jewish girl living in Amsterdam during the Second World War. She got a red checked diary for her 13th birthday in June 1942. Weeks later, her family went into hiding from the Nazis in rooms behind her father's office.

For more than two years she wrote about fear, boredom, quarrels, hopes and growing up. Many entries begin "Dear Kitty". In 1944 the family was discovered, and Anne died in a camp the next year, during the [[@holocaust|Holocaust]]. Her father survived and published the diary in 1947. It has since been read by millions in dozens of languages.

Babur, the first [[@mughals|Mughal]] emperor, wrote a memoir called the Baburnama in the early 1500s, partly based on day-by-day notes. He described battles, but also India's birds, fruits and rivers, and how much he missed the melons of Central Asia.

In America, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark kept journals as they crossed the continent between 1804 and 1806. Their notes on plants, animals and the [[@lewis-clark|lands they explored]] are still studied today.

Some people now keep diaries on phones or computers, or post short updates online. A private paper diary is different, because nobody else is reading. Many children start with a diary that has a little lock and key.

Writers often keep journals to collect ideas. Ruskin Bond, who has lived for decades in Landour, near Mussoorie, published one as *Landour Days: A Writer's Journal*. It is full of small things he noticed: rain on a tin roof, a bird at the window, a visit from a neighbour. Notes like these often grow into stories later.

Diaries also became a popular way to write stories. Jeff Kinney's *Diary of a Wimpy Kid*, first published in 2007, is told through a boy's doodle-filled journal, and it made millions of children want to start their own.

text: For about 3,000 years, the people of ancient Egypt believed that gods ran every part of life: the rising Sun, the Nile flood, birth, death and even beer-making. More than a thousand gods' names are known. Many had human bodies and animal heads, like Anubis with the head of a jackal, or Horus with the head of a falcon.

The Egyptians also believed that death was a journey to another life. A person who lived well, and whose body was carefully prepared, could reach a happy land of reeds and fields. That belief explains [[@mummies|mummies]], tombs packed with goods, and the pyramids themselves.

Most Egyptians saw animals as signs or homes of a god's power, not as gods themselves. A cat could stand for the goddess Bastet, much as a statue or image represents a god in other religions.

sec.t:
To the Egyptians, the Sun god Ra sailed across the sky each day in a boat. At sunset he entered the Duat, the underworld, and travelled through it all night.

There, a giant serpent called Apep waited to swallow him. Every night, Ra and his helpers fought Apep off. Every dawn, the Sun rose again because Ra had won. Priests chanted spells to help him. A sunrise wasn't something to take for granted.

The most famous Egyptian story is about a family. Osiris was a good king. His jealous brother Set killed him and scattered his body across Egypt.

Osiris's wife, Isis, searched the land and gathered the pieces. With magic, she brought him back long enough to have a son, Horus. Osiris became ruler of the dead. Horus grew up, fought Set for the throne and lost an eye in battle, which was magically healed. The "Eye of Horus" became a symbol of protection, and you can still see it on jewellery today.

Every pharaoh was said to be Horus on Earth, and became Osiris after death.

When someone died, Egyptians believed they faced a test in the Hall of Truth. Anubis placed the dead person's heart on one side of a scale and a feather on the other. The feather stood for Maat, the goddess of truth and order.

If the heart balanced, the person went on to the afterlife. If it was heavier, Ammit, a monster with a crocodile's head, a lion's front and a hippo's back, gobbled it up. To help, families buried the dead with spells written on papyrus in [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]]. We call these collections the Book of the Dead.

sec.h: Cats, crocodiles and millions of mummies
sec.t:
Animals carried a god's power. Cats were linked with Bastet, a goddess of home and protection. Crocodiles belonged to Sobek, and ibis birds to Thoth, the god of writing.

People bought mummified animals as offerings, and some temples held them in staggering numbers. Millions of mummified ibises have been found in underground galleries at Saqqara. In 1888, a farmer found a huge cat cemetery, and tens of thousands of cat mummies were shipped to England, where many were ground up as fertiliser.

Most Egyptian beliefs come back to the river. The Nile flooded each summer and left rich black mud for farming. Egyptians linked this to the god Hapi, and to tears of Isis mourning Osiris. Their whole year was built around the flood, which you can follow in the story of [[@egypt-nile|the Nile]].

When the Greeks later ruled Egypt, they met these gods and saw their own in them. They matched Thoth with Hermes and Ra with Helios. The idea of judging a person's deeds after death also turns up in many other traditions, from the court of Yama in Hindu stories to the scales in medieval European paintings. Whether those [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]] borrowed more than names from Egypt is a question historians still enjoy arguing about.

text: The Vikram and Betal stories are a set of old Indian tales tied together by one bigger story. A wise king named Vikram promises a holy man that he will bring him a body hanging from a tree in a cremation ground. But inside the body lives a vetala, or Betal, a spirit who loves to talk.

As Vikram walks back with Betal on his shoulder, Betal tells him a story that ends in a puzzle. If Vikram knows the answer, he must say it, or his head will burst. But the moment he speaks, Betal flies back to the tree. So it happens again and again, through 25 stories.

st.prompt: Betal warns King Vikram about his riddles. What will happen if Vikram knows the answer but stays silent?

options.t: His head will burst into a thousand pieces
He will be turned into a bat
He will forget his own name

st.reveal: That is the trap. If Vikram speaks, Betal escapes back to the tree. If he knows the answer and keeps quiet, his head will shatter. So the honest, clever king answers every time, and has to trudge back for Betal again.

src: Somadeva, Kathasaritsagara (Ocean of the Streams of Stories), translated by C. H. Tawney.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Vetalapanchavimshati.
n.certNote: The stories are very old, but the king's identity is not settled. The oldest Sanskrit versions name a king called Trivikramasena, while later retellings made him the legendary Vikramaditya of Ujjain, who may be based on more than one real ruler.

myth: The Vikram and Betal stories were made up for children's comics and TV.
They are hundreds of years old and were first written down in Sanskrit for grown-up readers. Comics like Chandamama and the 1985 TV series retold them for families much later.

the Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva and the Brihatkathamanjari of Kshemendra, 11th century, Kashmir

sec.h: A story that holds other stories

sec.t:
Each tale ends with a question that sounds simple but isn't. In one, three young men help bring a girl back to life. One carried her bones to a holy river, one stayed beside her ashes, and one found a mantra that restored her. Who should marry her? Vikram reasons that the one who gave her life acted like a father, and the one who carried her bones acted like a son. The one who stayed beside her, out of love, acted like a husband.

In another, a woman's husband and brother lose their heads, and a goddess lets her put them back. In her hurry, she joins each head to the wrong body. Which one is now her husband? Vikram says the man with her husband's head, because the head rules the body. This tale inspired a novel by Thomas Mann and Girish Karnad's play Hayavadana.

Vikram could simply give up and go home, but he never does. In the stories, he has made a promise, and a good king keeps his word even when the job is hard and a little frightening. Each time Betal escapes, Vikram turns round, walks back through the dark, climbs the tree and lifts the spirit onto his shoulder again.

That stubbornness is part of the fun. Listeners know exactly what will happen at the end of each tale, yet they still lean in to hear the riddle. The repeated pattern, a story, a question, an answer and an escape, makes the collection easy to remember and to retell around a lamp at night.

In the 25th story, Betal finally asks a question Vikram can't answer. It involves a father and son who marry a daughter and her mother, and asks how their children would be related. Vikram thinks hard and stays silent, and his head does not burst, because he honestly does not know.

Pleased, Betal reveals a secret. The holy man plans to sacrifice Vikram to gain magic powers. Thanks to the warning, Vikram turns the tables on the holy man and survives, and the king is promised that these tales will be remembered.

For many Indian children, Vikram and Betal arrived through [[@chandamama|Chandamama]] magazine, which ran the tales for decades with a famous picture of the king carrying the spirit. Later, Amar Chitra Katha comics retold them too.

In 1985, Doordarshan aired the TV serial Vikram aur Betaal, made by Ramanand Sagar. In those days India had one main channel, so whole families and neighbours gathered to watch, like the [[@tv-shows-india|shows]] that followed it. Many grown-ups still remember Betal's laugh and the line warning Vikram that his head would shatter. These [[@riddles|riddles]] have lasted because they make listeners argue, and an argument keeps a story alive.

text: In the United States, barbecue means cooking meat very slowly, with low heat and the smoke from burning wood. A cook, called a pitmaster, might keep a pork shoulder or a beef brisket at around 110 to 135 °C for ten hours or more. The meat comes out dark outside, pink just under the surface, and soft enough to pull apart with a fork.

Barbecue is popular because it turns cheap, tough cuts into something delicious, and because it is a social food. It has long been the centrepiece of church picnics, political rallies, family reunions and Fourth of July parties. Each region of the South is fiercely proud of its own style.

st.prompt: Why do barbecue cooks use low heat for many hours instead of high heat for a short time?

options.t: Slow heat melts the tough connective tissue in cheap cuts of meat
High heat would set the smoke on fire
Low heat kills more germs

st.reveal: Tough cuts like brisket and pork shoulder are full of collagen, a stringy protein. Long, gentle heat turns it into soft gelatin, so the meat becomes tender instead of chewy.

src: Moss R.F., Barbecue. The History of an American Institution. University of Alabama Press, 2010.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Barbecue.
n.certNote: The cooking itself is well understood. Where the word "barbecue" comes from is less certain, though most experts trace it to a Caribbean word recorded by Spanish explorers.

d.try: Run a sauce taste test at home with an adult. Mix one spoon of tomato ketchup with half a spoon of vinegar, and another spoon of ketchup with half a spoon of honey. Dip cucumber or bread in each and vote on which you prefer. You have just tasted the difference between a sharp Carolina-style sauce and a sweet Kansas City one.
myth: Barbecue and grilling are the same thing.

Grilling cooks food quickly over high, direct heat, like a burger on a hot grate. Barbecue cooks meat slowly with low heat and wood smoke, often for many hours. Many Americans still call any outdoor cookout a "barbecue", which adds to the confusion.

sec.t:
The meat used in barbecue comes from hard-working muscles, like the chest or shoulder of a cow or pig. These are full of [[collagen|collagen]], a tough protein that holds muscle fibres together. Cook them fast and they turn rubbery.

Cook them slowly, though, and the collagen gradually melts into soft gelatin. Fat melts too and keeps the meat moist. The smoke adds flavour and a pinkish "smoke ring" just under the crust, made when gases from the fire react with the meat. Wood choice matters: hickory, oak, pecan and, in Texas, mesquite each give a different taste. The [[@cooking-science|science of cooking]] here is mostly about patience.

In the American South, much of the actual pit work for big barbecues was done by enslaved African Americans, and later by Black cooks and pitmasters. They dug the pits, tended the fires through the night and developed many of the techniques still used. Historians now say that the story of barbecue cannot be told without them.

In the 20th century, decades after the end of [[@slavery-freedom|slavery]], millions of Black Americans moved north in search of work and fairer treatment. They carried barbecue to cities such as Chicago and Kansas City, where it took new forms.

Barbecue fans argue endlessly about whose is best. In the Carolinas, the favourite is pork, often a whole hog, with a thin, sharp vinegar sauce. In Memphis, Tennessee, people love pork ribs rubbed with dry spices. In Kansas City, almost any meat goes on, covered in thick, sweet [[@food-ketchup-history|tomato sauce]].

In central [[@texas|Texas]], the king is beef brisket, seasoned with little more than salt and [[@cardamom-pepper|black pepper]]. Famous Texas barbecue joints often sell out by early afternoon, and people queue for hours.

India has its own long tradition of cooking with fire and smoke, though usually faster and hotter. A tandoor, a clay oven, reaches far higher temperatures than an American barbecue pit, cooking naan and tikka in minutes. Seekh kebabs sizzle over glowing coals in Lucknow and Old Delhi, and bhutta, roasted corn, is sold on street corners each monsoon. The goal is different, but the love of smoke and flame is shared.

text: India has more than a thousand kinds of mango for two reasons. People have grown mangoes here for thousands of years, across very different climates. And a mango stone almost never grows into a copy of its parent.

Each seed carries a new mix of [[@genes-family|genes]] from two parent trees, the way brothers and sisters differ. So every seedling tree is a little experiment. When one gave delicious fruit, farmers kept it going by [[grafting|grafting]], joining its twigs onto young roots. Over centuries, in thousands of villages, that produced Alphonso, Kesar, Dasheri, Langra, Banganapalli, Himsagar, Totapuri and hundreds more, each with its own colour, shape, smell and taste.

st.prompt: How do farmers make sure a new tree gives exactly the same mangoes as a favourite old tree?

options.t: They join a cutting from the old tree onto a young tree's roots
They plant a stone from the old tree's best mango
They water the new tree with the same well water

st.reveal: This is called grafting. A twig or bud from the old tree is joined to a young seedling so the two grow together. The fruit then comes from the old tree's twig, so it matches exactly. Planting a stone gives a tree with its own mix of genes.

src: ICAR, Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture, Lucknow, mango.
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, FAOSTAT crop production.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, mango.
n.certNote: India clearly has a huge number of mango varieties, but counts range from about 1,000 to more than 1,500, depending on how local types are counted and named.

d.try: Hold a mango tasting at home in the season. Get two or three different kinds, cut them, and note the colour of the flesh, how stringy it is, how sweet or sour it tastes and what the smell reminds you of. Give each a score out of ten and see if your family agrees.
myth: If you plant the stone of a great mango, you'll get a tree with the same great mangoes.

Most Indian mango varieties don't grow true from seed, because each stone carries a new mix of genes from two parent trees. The fruit can be very different. That's why farmers graft to copy good trees, and also why new varieties keep appearing.
facts: for at least a few thousand years
Mangoes from India allowed into the USA again

sec.t:
The wild mango comes from the region around northeast India, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Mangoes appear in old Sanskrit and Tamil writing and in Buddhist stories, and the [[@mango-tree|mango tree]] is sacred in many Hindu traditions. It is India's [[@national-symbols|national fruit]].

India is by far the world's largest grower. In the early 2020s it produced roughly two-fifths of all the mangoes grown on Earth, though most are eaten inside India rather than exported.

The Alphonso, called Hapus in Marathi, is named after Afonso de Albuquerque, a Portuguese commander in [[@goa|Goa]] in the early 1500s. The [[@portuguese-india|Portuguese]] are often credited with spreading grafting along India's west coast. Alphonsos from Ratnagiri and Devgad in Maharashtra are now protected with a GI tag, a label that says a product really comes from a particular place.

Scientists also create new kinds on purpose. In the 1970s, researchers in New Delhi crossed the Dasheri with the Neelam to produce the Amrapali, a small tree that suits home gardens and gives fruit every year.

Because India is so big, mango season moves across the map. The first fruit often arrive from the south as early as March. Alphonsos peak in April and May, Kesar and Dasheri in early summer, and Chausa and Fazli can last into July and August.

Each region swears its own is best. Gujarat has Kesar from the slopes near Gir, Andhra Pradesh has Banganapalli and Bengal has Himsagar. The stringy Totapuri, shaped like a parrot's beak, goes into much of the mango pulp sold in cartons.

Mangoes are eaten unripe too. Raw green mango goes into pickles, chutneys, cooling aam panna and the sour powder called amchur.

Most mangoes in American shops are grown in Mexico and Central and South America. A popular kind, the Tommy Atkins, has a tough skin that travels well. Its family tree goes back to Florida in the early 1900s, and to an Indian variety brought there as a young grafted tree.

Indian mangoes were barred from the United States for years because of worries about insect pests. In 2007 the ban was lifted for fruit treated to kill any insects, and Alphonso and Kesar boxes began arriving in Indian grocery shops across the country.

text: Rice is the seed of a grass. Each plant makes a few hundred grains, and a single hectare of good paddy, about the size of a football field and a half, can produce several tonnes. It keeps for months once dried, cooks quickly and fills you up.

That is why rice became the main food for more than half the people on Earth, especially in Asia, where about 90% of it is grown and eaten. India and [[@china-today|China]] grow the most. In the 2024–25 season India overtook China as the biggest grower, and India also sells more rice to other countries than anyone else.

st.prompt: Rice can grow in dry fields too. So why do most farmers flood their paddies?

options.t: The water drowns weeds that would compete with the rice
Rice seeds only sprout underwater
Flooding keeps birds from eating the grains

st.reveal: Rice copes with standing water because it pipes air down to its roots. Most weeds can't, so the flood does the weeding. Some farmers grow "upland" rice on dry hillsides, but yields are usually lower.

International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), rice basics.
Britannica, rice.

myth: Rice has to grow underwater.
Rice can grow in ordinary wet soil. Flooding mainly stops weeds and makes water easy to control. Upland rice, grown on dry slopes, is still farmed in parts of India and Africa.

sec.h: From wild grass to dinner plate
sec.t:
People in the Yangtze River valley in China began farming rice about 9,000 years ago. Over thousands of years they chose plants whose grains did not fall off before harvest. Rice reached India early, and Indian farmers grew their own kinds in the wet Ganga plains.

In West Africa, people tamed a separate species of rice on their own, about 3,000 years ago. Enslaved Africans later brought their rice-growing skills to South Carolina in the USA, where rice made plantation owners rich. Today the US state of Arkansas grows about half of America's rice.

In the 1960s, India was short of food and had to import grain. Scientists at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines bred a short, sturdy rice called IR8, released in 1966. It grew more grain and did not fall over when heavy with seed.

Along with new wheat, fertiliser and irrigation, this was part of the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]]. Within a few decades India went from buying grain to selling it. The changes also used much more water and chemicals, a problem farmers are still dealing with.

A rice grain is wrapped in a tough husk, which mills remove. Underneath is brown rice, still coated in bran. Polishing rubs away the bran and the germ, leaving white rice, which cooks faster and keeps longer but loses some vitamins.

There are tens of thousands of varieties. Long, fragrant basmati grows in the foothills of the Himalayas. Sticky rice holds together for eating with your fingers in [[@thailand|Thailand]] and Laos. Short, round grains go into Japanese [[@sushi|sushi]] and the payasam of Kerala.

Rice also travels well as a dry food. Flattened rice, called [[@indian-breakfasts|poha]] or aval, is made by soaking, roasting and pressing the grains. Puffed rice, or murmura, pops when grains are heated in hot sand. Both turn up in snacks from Kolkata's jhalmuri to Mumbai's bhel puri, and both keep for weeks in a tin.

Flooded paddies have a hidden side effect. Microbes in the airless mud make methane, a gas that traps heat in the air, so rice farming adds to [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Some farmers now let their fields dry out for a few days between [[@floods-why|floods]]. It saves water and cuts methane, and the rice still grows.

text: Indian street food is cheap, quick and full of strong flavours: [[@tamarind|sour tamarind]], sweet chutney, spicy green chilli, crunchy sev and cooling curd, often in a single bite. It's cooked fresh in front of you by vendors who may have made the same snack for decades.

Every region has its own specialities. Mumbai has vada pav and pav bhaji, Delhi has chole bhature and aloo tikki, [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] has kathi rolls and jhalmuri, and Indore is famous for its night market. Street food also tells a story about history. Many snacks were invented to feed workers, travellers and students who needed a filling meal for a few rupees.

st.prompt: Where does the word "chaat" come from?

options.t: A Hindi word meaning "to lick"
A Persian word meaning "small"
The name of a famous cook

st.reveal: Chaat comes from chaatna, to lick. It's a cheerful name for food so tangy and saucy that people lick their fingers clean afterwards.

src: Government of India, Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014.

UNESCO, Hawker culture in Singapore (2020).
n.certNote: Many street foods have origin stories that are passed on by word of mouth, such as pav bhaji being created for Mumbai's mill workers. Historians have only limited written records to check them.

d.try: Make a street food map of India. Draw a rough outline of the country and mark at least eight cities. Next to each, draw or write one street food it is famous for. Ask family members from different states to add their favourites.
myth: Street food is always less safe than restaurant food.

Safety depends on clean water, clean hands and freshly cooked food, not on whether it is sold from a cart or a kitchen. Food fried or cooked hot in front of you is often fine. India's food safety agency trains vendors and certifies clean street food hubs.

sec.t:
[[@chaat|Chaat]] is a family of tangy snacks. Papdi chaat piles crisp wafers with potato, chickpeas, curd and chutneys. Bhel puri mixes puffed rice, onion, tomato and sev. The name comes from the Hindi word *chaatna*, to lick.

A well-loved legend traces chaat to Mughal [[@delhi|Delhi]]. It says the emperor Shah Jahan's physician told people to eat spicy, fried food to protect themselves from the river water. There's no clear proof for this story. But Old Delhi's lanes, near the Red Fort, are still famous for their chaat.

Hollow, crisp puris filled with spiced water are called [[@pani-puri|pani puri]] in Mumbai, golgappa in Delhi and much of north India, and puchka in Kolkata. In Kolkata, the filling is often sharper and the potato more mashed. In Mumbai, there's sweet chutney too.

Arguments about whose version is best are a national pastime. Each city's version reflects local tastes, from the tamarind of the south to the spicy mint water of the north. Most of these snacks rely on [[@chillies|chillies]], which came to India only about 500 years ago.

Many famous street foods were created for people on the move. Pav bhaji, a spicy mashed vegetable curry eaten with buttered bread, is said to have been invented in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] for textile mill workers who needed a quick dinner late at night. Vada pav, a potato fritter in a bun, fed the same workers in the 1960s.

Kolkata's kathi roll, a paratha wrapped around kebabs, is often traced to a restaurant called Nizam's, which opened in the 1930s. [[@food-momos|Momos]], the steamed dumplings, came to India from Tibet and [[@nepal|Nepal]], and spread from Darjeeling and the Northeast to cities across the country. Mumbai's workers also rely on the [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawalas]] for home food.

[[@food-street-food-world|Street food]] isn't only Indian. In [[@singapore|Singapore]], hawker centres, open food courts full of stalls, are so loved that UNESCO added hawker culture to its heritage list in 2020. In the USA, food trucks sell [[@tacos|tacos]] in Los Angeles and halal food in New York.

{{story:shops-markets}}

India has many millions of [[@people-street-vendors|street vendors]]. For years, many faced fines and were moved on by officials. In 2014, [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] passed a law to protect their right to earn a living and to set aside vending zones in cities.

India's food safety agency also runs a programme that trains vendors in hygiene, such as using clean water, gloves and covered food. Streets that pass are certified as "clean street food hubs". Many famous food lanes, from Mumbai to Bhopal, have joined.

Street food is often the first place to try a city's flavours. You eat standing up, shoulder to shoulder with office workers, students and families, all for a small price. It changes with the seasons, too: hot corn in the monsoon, gajak and hot [[@food-jalebi|jalebis]] in a Delhi winter, kulfi in the heat of May. A good vendor remembers how spicy you like it.

text: A taco is a small, soft tortilla wrapped or folded around a filling. In Mexico the tortilla is usually [[@corn-maize|made of corn]], warmed on a flat griddle called a comal, much like a tawa. On top go meat, beans, cheese or vegetables, then fresh onion, coriander, a squeeze of lime fruit and a spoonful of salsa.

Tacos are everyday [[@food-street-food-world|street food]] across [[@mexico|Mexico]]. Stands sell them from morning until late at night, often for a few pesos each. They are eaten standing up, [[@food-eating-with-hands|with your hands]], and the trick is to tip your head sideways so nothing falls out. Anyone who has eaten a kathi roll in Kolkata knows the feeling.

st.prompt: Before grinding corn for tortillas, Mexican cooks soak and cook it in water mixed with what?

options.t: Lime, a mineral powder from limestone
Lemon juice
Salt and sugar

st.reveal: The "lime" here is calcium hydroxide, called cal in Mexico, not the fruit. It softens the corn's hard skin and frees up a B vitamin called niacin that the body could not otherwise use.

src: Pilcher J.M., Planet Taco. A Global History of Mexican Food. Oxford University Press, 2012.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Corn; Nixtamalization.
n.certNote: The food and its ingredients are well understood. Where the word "taco" comes from is uncertain, and historians have several competing ideas.

d.try: Compare flatbreads. Ask an adult at home or a friend's family for one corn roti (makki ki roti), one wheat chapati and one rice bhakri or a tortilla if you can find one. Fold each in half and note which cracks, which bends, and which smells sweetest.
myth: Real Mexican tacos come in crunchy, U-shaped shells.
In Mexico, most tacos are soft corn tortillas folded around a filling. Pre-made crispy shells became famous through fast-food restaurants in the United States from the 1950s and 1960s.

sec.t:
Corn, or maize, was first farmed in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago, from a wild grass called teosinte with tiny, hard ears. Over thousands of years, farmers chose the best plants and seeds, and the ears grew bigger and softer. Corn became the most important food of the [[@aztecs-maya|Aztecs, the Maya]] and many other peoples.

A [[@myths-maya|Maya creation story]] even says the first humans were made from maize dough. Corn was eaten at almost every meal, and the tortilla was the plate, [[@food-cutlery-history|spoon]] and bread all in one.

Mexican tacos change from region to region. Carnitas is slow-cooked pork. Barbacoa is meat steamed for hours, traditionally in a pit. Baja California, on the Pacific coast, is famous for fried fish tacos.

Tacos al pastor have a surprising story. In the early 20th century, immigrants from Lebanon brought shawarma to Mexico: meat stacked on a tall turning spit and sliced thin. Mexican cooks swapped lamb for pork, added chilli and pineapple, and put the slices in tortillas. The spit is called a trompo, meaning [[@yo-yo-tops|spinning top]].

Nobody is sure where the word "taco" comes from. One idea, put forward by the historian Jeffrey Pilcher, links it to silver mines of the 1700s, where a "taco" was a paper-wrapped charge used for blasting rock. Others think the word simply meant a plug or wad, something rolled up. The name is younger than the food, which is thousands of years old.

In the United States, Mexican American cooks were frying tortillas into crisp shells by the early 1900s. In the 1950s, restaurant owners found ways to make pre-shaped U-shaped shells, which could be filled quickly. [[@fast-food-history|Fast-food chains]], such as Taco Bell, which opened in 1962, made them famous across the country.

Those shells are a big part of [[@tex-mex|Tex-Mex]] food today. Many Mexicans think of them as a foreign idea, which is a funny fate for a dish named in [[@spanish-language|Spanish]].
